title: Efficient average-distortion embeddings of polyhedral norms
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time construction of a globally defined Euclidean embedding of the square-root metric of every rational polyhedral norm, with quadratic average distortion at most \(C\sqrt{\log_2 d}\) on any given finite rational point set, for one universal constant \(C\)? The construction must produce a finite description permitting polynomial-time evaluation to any requested precision. This is the explicitly encoded polyhedral-norm branch of the source’s algorithmic average-John question; the exact guarantees and complexity parameters are below.
why: Average-distance preservation can be much better than preservation of every distance from below. Constructing such maps would make a strong structural theorem in metric geometry algorithmically usable. The global nonexpansion requirement matters because a later query point need not belong to the original data set.
status_note: The broader constructive question is open in the 2021 seminar source. This card explicitly fixes a rational polyhedral bit-model specialization. Checked later sketching results have different output and nonexpansion guarantees, but bounded checks through 2026-09-16 do not independently establish current openness of this selected computational version.

progress.text: Naor’s published average John theorem establishes the geometric \(O(\sqrt{\log d})\) bound through an existence argument.
The seminar report asks for an explicit efficient map, and the near-neighbor paper gives constructions for specified norm families.

Version 3 of the average-distortion sketching preprint develops a more general sketch-and-decoder model and results for discrete subsets of fixed norm families. These guarantees are not the global Euclidean-map target.

sentences: The average John theorem preserves squared distances on average after taking the square root of a norm metric.
The algorithmic question asks for an efficiently constructed map that is nonexpanding on the entire space, including future query points.
This card explicitly selects rational polyhedral norms and rational data points so that the input and computational cost have finite bit encodings.
The output must describe one continuous Euclidean map that can be evaluated to any requested precision in polynomial time.
This would turn a structural existence theorem into an algorithmic object, while the present review keeps the current status of the selected computational specialization uncertain.

definitions:
An input consists of integers \(d\ge2\), \(r\ge d\), \(n\ge2\), a matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{r\times d}\) of column rank \(d\), and a list \(P=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of pairwise distinct points in \(\mathbb Q^d\). Integers and rational coordinates are written in binary, with signed numerators and positive denominators; dimensions and lists are explicit. Let \(N\) be the total input bit length. Define a norm on the entire real space \(\mathbb R^d\) by
\[
\|x\|_A=\max_{1\le j\le r}|(Ax)_j|,
\qquad
\operatorname{dist}_A(x,y)=\sqrt{\|x-y\|_A}.
\]
Full column rank makes \(\|\cdot\|_A\) a norm. There is no bound on \(r\), coordinate magnitudes or geometric aspect ratios except what their input lengths express. The norm is supplied by the matrix, not by a unit-cost oracle. All arithmetic and norm evaluations are charged at bit cost.

The assertion asks for two fixed deterministic multitape Turing-machine programs \(B,E\), constants \(C,K\ge1\), and an integer \(a\ge1\), independent of every input. On each valid input, \(B\) must output an integer \(m\ge1\) and a finite binary description \(\sigma\) in at most \(K(N+1)^a\) steps, with \(m\) and \(|\sigma|\) at most \(K(N+1)^a\). That description must specify one continuous function \(f_\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
\|f_\sigma(x)-f_\sigma(y)\|_2^2\le\|x-y\|_A
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb R^d
\]
and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n
\|f_\sigma(p_i)-f_\sigma(p_j)\|_2^2
\ \ge\
\frac{1}{C^2\log_2 d}
\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\|p_i-p_j\|_A.
\]
Here \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is the Euclidean norm. Both sums are over ordered pairs, including the zero diagonal. The average is with respect to the uniform distribution on \(P\); the factor \(n^{-2}\) cancels on both sides. The first inequality is nonexpansion for the square-root metric on the whole space, including points outside \(P\). The second controls squared Euclidean distances on average. No individual lower bound on a pairwise distance or injectivity is required.

The meaning of a finite description is fixed by the second program. On input \((\sigma,x,1^k)\), where \(x\in\mathbb Q^d\) has binary description length \(b\) and \(k\ge1\), \(E\) must output a dyadic rational vector \(v\in\mathbb Q^m\) satisfying
\[
\|v-f_\sigma(x)\|_2\le2^{-k}
\]
in at most \(K(N+b+k+1)^a\) bit operations. Dyadic rationals are represented by an integer numerator and a power-of-two denominator, both explicitly encoded in binary. The approximations for all rational \(x\) and all precisions must correspond to the same continuous map; they are not separate independently chosen embeddings. Continuity and density of rational points determine that map on all of \(\mathbb R^d\). Its displayed geometric inequalities are exact mathematical requirements; rounding pertains only to evaluation.

The description may include the original matrix and point set. Both construction and evaluation may depend polynomially on their total bit length; no storage or query-time bound independent of \(n\) is imposed. No random bits, advice, noncomputable real constants, free preprocessing or oracle is available. The problem asks for construction of a map, not just a table of images of the input points.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of such uniform programs and constants, including their bit complexity, a single well-defined global map per output description, both geometric inequalities and the evaluation guarantee at every rational query and precision, or a complete Lean proof that the assertion is false. A nonconstructive embedding, a map defined only on \(P\), or a sketch whose decoder estimates distances without giving Euclidean coordinates does not meet this target. The distortion requirement is \(O(\sqrt{\log d})\) with a common constant; \(2^{-k}\) specifies computational output precision. Neither is replaced by the numerical-benchmark \(1/100\) tolerance.

context_blocks.text: Nikolov’s question in Section 4.3 starts with the square-root metric of a finite-dimensional normed space and asks for an explicit, efficiently computable average-distortion map from the given point set. The preceding existence theorem already supplies the geometric distortion bound.

The report does not specify how an arbitrary norm is encoded or how real-valued outputs are represented. This card explicitly selects rational polyhedral norms given by a full-rank matrix and rational data points, and uses finite descriptions with certified precision-dependent evaluation. This is a documented computational specialization, not a claim of equivalence to all norm-oracle formulations of the original question.

The selected efficiency requirement is polynomial in the full input bit length, including the norm description. It does not impose the stronger succinct storage and query bounds, independent of the number of data points, used by some near-neighbor-search reductions. Those bounds are a separate requirement.

Naor’s average John theorem gives a map from the whole normed space into a Hilbert space with quadratic average distortion \(O(\sqrt{\log d})\) for its one-half snowflake. The theorem and its discussion distinguish this existence statement from an explicit efficient construction.

Kush, Nikolov and Tang give explicit average-distortion embeddings for \(\ell_p\) spaces and a framework relating efficient embeddings to near-neighbor search. Their stated special-case constructions do not supply the full polynomial-time map required here for arbitrary input polyhedral norms.

The 2025 average-distortion sketching paper permits an arbitrary compressed representation and a pairwise distance decoder. Its nonexpansion guarantee is stated in expectation over sketches; this is distinct from one globally nonexpanding map into a Euclidean space.

checked_sources: Read Dagstuhl Seminar 21181 Section 4.3, printed page 18, including the all-domain Lipschitz requirement and the squared-distance average. The inherited PDF page locator referred to the combined issue rather than the report’s printed page.

Read Naor’s author PDF Theorem 1 and surrounding discussion, pages 1–2; verified publication and arXiv revision dates. The target is constructive efficiency, not the already-proved existence of a Hilbert-space embedding.

Read Kush–Nikolov–Tang arXiv:2105.04712v1 Definition 2, Theorems 5–6 and the general-norm discussion on pages 4–7. Distinguished the source’s succinct NNS conditions from this explicitly selected polynomial-total-input formulation.

Read average-distortion sketching arXiv:2411.05156v3 Section 1.2 Definition 1.1 and comparison with embeddings and checked the stated contribution scope in Section 1.3. A randomized sketch with a distance decoder need not be a globally nonexpanding Euclidean map.

Model check: rank d makes max_j |(Ax)_j| a norm, and the displayed first inequality is exactly nonexpansion for its one-half snowflake. Uniform rational-query approximations plus continuity specify at most one map on the entire real domain. The second inequality uses the original norm to the first power because the source metric is square-rooted.

Bounded later searches through 2026-09-16 verified no complete algorithm or lower bound for this explicit finite-description branch. The report leaves representation unspecified, so this review does not certify the selected specialization as a currently open theorem. No full proof verification of later results or Lean formalization is claimed.
